# Welcome {-}  
  
These notes present an introduction to **portfolio theory** — the  
framework for understanding how investors should and do combine assets  
to manage risk and return.  
  
## What this book covers  
  
- **Chapter \@ref(chap-intro) — Introduction**: portfolio theory as a  
  descriptive and normative theory, the "do not put all your eggs in  
  one basket" principle, the origins of mean-variance analysis with  
  Markowitz, and the role of investor psychology (bubbles, animal  
  spirits, heuristics).  
- **Chapter \@ref(chap-risk) — Risks on Investments**: the concept of  
  risk and the risk–return trade-off, the major sources of risk  
  (business, financial, purchasing power, interest rate, liquidity,  
  tax, market, and event risk), and the distinction between  
  diversifiable and non-diversifiable risk.  
- **Chapter \@ref(chap-capm) — Capital Asset Pricing Model**: the  
  development of the CAPM by Sharpe, Lintner, and Mossin, its  
  assumptions and practical implications, the security market line,  
  and the beta factor.  
- **Chapter \@ref(chap-portfolio) — Diversification and Portfolio  
  Theory**: systematic versus specific risk, volatility and value,  
  uncorrelated returns, two-asset portfolios, short sales, the  
  efficient frontier, and the capital market line.  
- **Chapter \@ref(chap-capm-practice) — CAPM in Practice**: the  
  components of required return under CAPM, five methods for  
  calculating beta with worked illustrations, portfolio betas, gearing  
  and ungeared/geared betas, the alpha factor, limitations of the  
  CAPM, and the Arbitrage Pricing Theory as a multi-factor  
  alternative.  
- **Appendix**: a summary of all key formulas and full references.  
  
## Conventions used {-}  
  
Worked illustrations appear in *example* boxes and are numbered  
(Illustration 1–7). Equations, tables, and figures are numbered and  
cross-referenced throughout the text. Key definitions and results are  
set in *definition*, *theorem*, and *note* blocks.  
  
:::{.rmdnote}  
Solutions to the worked examples assume cash flows occur at the end of  
the stated period, and rounding differences of a few kobo may appear  
in NPV calculations.  
:::
